claim: The efficient-coding hypothesis predicts that neuronal population responses should be sparse.
source: The efficient-coding hypothesis is an important organizing principle of any sensory system (Barlow, 1981; Olshausen and Field, 1996). It predicts that neuronal population responses should be sparse, although the optimal level of sparseness depends on many factors.
evidence: Supported by citations to Barlow (1981) and Olshausen and Field (1996)

claim: Most experimental evidence of sparse coding comes from responses of individual neurons exposed to large sets of natural image stimuli, measured using single-unit recording techniques.
source: Most of the experimental evidence of sparse coding comes from the responses of individual neurons that were exposed to a large set of natural image stimuli, measured using single-unit recording techniques (Haider et al., 2010; Hromádka et al., 2008; Rust and DiCarlo, 2012; Vinje and Gallant, 2000).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior studies

claim: The first direct measurement of population response sparseness was performed with two-photon GCaMP6 signal imaging in rodents.
source: The first direct measurement of population response sparseness was performed with two-photon (2P) GCaMP6 signal imaging in rodents (Froudarakis et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Froudarakis et al., 2014

claim: GCaMP6 responses are subject to saturation at neuronal firing rates above 60–80 Hz.
source: One potential confound in this work, however, is that GCaMP6 responses are subject to saturation at neuronal firing rates above 60–80 Hz (Chen et al., 2013; Froudarakis et al., 2014), leading to the potential to under-estimate the sparseness measures that can capture the peakedness or sharpness of the population response distributions.
evidence: Supported by citations to Chen et al., 2013 and Froudarakis et al., 2014

claim: GCaMP5 exhibits linear non-saturating responses across a wide range of firing rates (10–150 Hz).
source: We showed previously that GCaMP5 exhibits linear non-saturating responses across a wide range of firing rates (10–150 Hz) (Li et al., 2017), allowing us to measure accurately the response sparseness of almost all of the neurons in layer two in V1 within a 850 µm x 850 µm field of view—the spatial scale of about one hypercolumn.
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al., 2017

claim: The study recorded neuronal population calcium responses to 2250 natural images in V1 layer two in two awake macaques.
source: Our 2P imaging of GCaMP5 recorded neuronal population calcium (Ca2+) responses to 2250 natural images in V1 layer two in two awake macaques (about 1000 neurons each).
evidence: Direct statement of experimental design and data collection

claim: The receptive field centers of the imaged neurons were located between 3° and 5° in eccentricity.
source: The RF centers of the imaged neurons were located between 3o and 5o in eccentricity.
evidence: Direct measurement reported in the study

claim: Natural images evoked robust visual responses in the imaged neurons.
source: These natural images evoked robust visual responses in the imaged neurons (Figure 1a,b, Figure 1—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Supported by data shown in figures

claim: Only a few neurons among nearly 1000 neurons measured responded strongly to a single patch of natural scenes.
source: Typically, only a few neurons, among the nearly 1000 neurons measured (1225 neurons for Monkey A or 982 neurons for Monkey B), responded strongly to a single patch of natural scenes.
evidence: Observation from experimental data shown in Figure 1

claim: 1225 neurons were recorded from monkey A.
source: We recorded data from 1225 neurons in monkey A and 982 neurons in monkey B, and found that only a few neurons in each monkey responded strongly to any given image (Figure 1a,b), though most of the neurons responded strongly to at least one of the images in the set (Figure 1c).

claim: 982 neurons were recorded from monkey B.
source: We recorded data from 1225 neurons in monkey A and 982 neurons in monkey B, and found that only a few neurons in each monkey responded strongly to any given image (Figure 1a,b), though most of the neurons responded strongly to at least one of the images in the set (Figure 1c).

claim: Most neurons responded strongly to at least one of the images in the set.
source: We recorded data from 1225 neurons in monkey A and 982 neurons in monkey B, and found that only a few neurons in each monkey responded strongly to any given image (Figure 1a,b), though most of the neurons responded strongly to at least one of the images in the set (Figure 1c).

claim: The rank-ordered distributions of the population responses were always sharply peaked.
source: The rank-ordered distributions of the population responses were always sharply peaked (Figure 1d,e).
evidence: Observation from data shown in figures

claim: On average, 0.49% of neurons responded above each's half-maximum for monkey A.
source: On average, the percentage of neurons that responded above each's half-maximum was 0.49% (6.0/1,225) for monkey A and and 0.42% (4.1/982) for monkey B (Figure 1f,g).

claim: On average, 0.42% of neurons responded above each's half-maximum for monkey B.
source: On average, the percentage of neurons that responded above each's half-maximum was 0.49% (6.0/1,225) for monkey A and and 0.42% (4.1/982) for monkey B (Figure 1f,g).

claim: Only about 0.5% of the cells responded strongly to each image, indicating a very high degree of sparseness in the strong population responses.
source: In other words, only about 0.5% of the cells responded strongly to each image, indicating a very high degree of sparseness in the strong population responses or a very sharp population response distribution.

claim: Most cells responded strongly to only a small number of images in the whole stimulus set.
source: Interestingly, we found that most cells responded strongly to only a small number of images in the whole stimulus set (Figure 2a,b).

claim: The preferred images for individual neurons often shared common features.
source: The preferred images for individual neurons often shared common features.
evidence: Observation from analysis of neuronal responses

claim: Neuron 653 of monkey A was most excited when its receptive field covered the lower rim of the cat's eye.
source: For example, neuron 653 of monkey A was most excited when its receptive field (0.8o in diameter) covered the lower rim of the cat's eye (indicated by the red dashed line in the inset in Figure 2b).

claim: The population average life-time sparseness was 0.49% (11/2,250) for Monkey A.
source: This population average was 0.49% (11/2,250) for Monkey A and 0.41% (9.3/2,250) for Monkey B (Figure 2e,f).

claim: The population average life-time sparseness was 0.41% (9.3/2,250) for Monkey B.
source: This population average was 0.49% (11/2,250) for Monkey A and 0.41% (9.3/2,250) for Monkey B (Figure 2e,f).

claim: A high degree of stimulus specificity or life-time sparseness goes hand-in-hand with a heightened population sparseness.
source: This suggests that a high degree of stimulus specificity or life-time sparseness goes hand-in-hand with a heightened population sparseness.
evidence: Inference drawn from the correlation between two measured quantities

claim: The entire population's decoding accuracy was 54% for Monkey A.
source: The entire population's decoding accuracy was 54% for Monkey A and 38% for Monkey B, whereas the chance accuracy was 0.04% (1/2,250) (Figure 3a,b, horizontal dashed lines).
evidence: Result from decoding analysis of experimental data

claim: The entire population's decoding accuracy was 38% for Monkey B.
source: The entire population's decoding accuracy was 54% for Monkey A and 38% for Monkey B, whereas the chance accuracy was 0.04% (1/2,250) (Figure 3a,b, horizontal dashed lines).
evidence: Result from decoding analysis of experimental data

claim: The chance accuracy for the decoding task was 0.04% (1/2,250).
source: The entire population's decoding accuracy was 54% for Monkey A and 38% for Monkey B, whereas the chance accuracy was 0.04% (1/2,250) (Figure 3a,b, horizontal dashed lines).

claim: A decoding accuracy of 28% for monkey A could be achieved with only the top 0.5% of the strongest signals included.
source: Remarkably, a decoding accuracy of 28% for monkey A and 21% for monkey B could be achieved with only the top 0.5% of the strongest signals included (Figure 3a,b vertical gray lines).

claim: A decoding accuracy of 21% for monkey B could be achieved with only the top 0.5% of the strongest signals included.
source: Remarkably, a decoding accuracy of 28% for monkey A and 21% for monkey B could be achieved with only the top 0.5% of the strongest signals included (Figure 3a,b vertical gray lines).

claim: Transmitting the top 0.5% of the strongest responses for each image was sufficient to realize 50% of the maximum achievable decoding performance for either monkey.
source: This means that transmitting the top 0.5% of the strongest responses for each image was sufficient to realize 50% of the maximum achievable decoding performance for either monkey.

claim: The decoding performance dropped by 50% when the strongest 0.5% of the signals are removed.
source: The intersections of the blue curves with the gray lines indicate that the decoding performance dropped by 50% when the strongest 0.5% of the signals are removed.
evidence: Result from decoding analysis shown in figures

claim: The top 0.5% of signals are both necessary and sufficient for realizing 50% of the decoding performance.
source: Thus, we showed that these strong and sparse signals contain the information necessary to realize half of the decoding performance.

claim: 99% of decoding performance is not reached until the top 40% (for monkey A) of the responses are included.
source: Although the top 0.5% of the signals are both necessary and sufficient for realizing 50% of the performance, 99% of decoding performance is not reached until the top 40% (for monkey A) and top 30% (for monkey B) of the responses are included (saturation of the red curves).

claim: 99% of decoding performance is not reached until the top 30% (for monkey B) of the responses are included.
source: Although the top 0.5% of the signals are both necessary and sufficient for realizing 50% of the performance, 99% of decoding performance is not reached until the top 40% (for monkey A) and top 30% (for monkey B) of the responses are included (saturation of the red curves).

claim: Without the top 5% responses, the decoding performance drops to practically zero.
source: However, without the top 5% responses, the decoding performance drops to practically zero (blue curve).

claim: The strongest 5% of the responses are necessary for the achievement of full performance, but insufficient by themselves.
source: Thus, the strongest 5% of the responses are necessary for the achievement of full performance, but insufficient by themselves.

claim: The presence of other weaker signals in the population is required to achieve the full performance.
source: In other words, the presence of other weaker signals in the population is required to achieve the full performance.

claim: Significant information contents are carried by the superb sparse strong responses.
source: The decoding results revealed that significant information contents are indeed carried by the superb sparse strong responses.

claim: This study provides the first direct measurement of population sparseness from V1 of awake macaques.
source: In this study, we provided the first direct measurement of population sparseness from V1 of awake macaques.
evidence: Statement of novelty of the study

claim: This study provides the first simultaneous recording of a large dense population of neurons in V1 at single-cell resolution in response to a large set of natural stimuli, using 2P imaging in awake macaque.
source: In conclusion, this study provides the first simultaneous recording of a large dense population of neurons in V1 at single-cell resolution in response to a large set of natural stimuli, using 2P imaging in awake macaque.
evidence: Statement of novelty of the study

claim: Earlier studies had provided life-time sparseness measurements in rodents.
source: Earlier studies had provided life-time sparseness measurements in rodents (Hromádka et al., 2008; Haider et al., 2010), non-human primates (Rolls and Tovee, 1995; Vinje and Gallant, 2000; Rust and DiCarlo, 2012) and humans (Quiroga et al., 2005), as well as population sparseness measurement in rodents (Froudarakis et al., 2014), but our study provides the first direct measurement of sparseness of large-scale neuronal population responses, carried out in awake macaque monkeys and made possible by large-scale 2P imaging techniques.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: Earlier studies had provided life-time sparseness measurements in non-human primates.
source: Earlier studies had provided life-time sparseness measurements in rodents (Hromádka et al., 2008; Haider et al., 2010), non-human primates (Rolls and Tovee, 1995; Vinje and Gallant, 2000; Rust and DiCarlo, 2012) and humans (Quiroga et al., 2005), as well as population sparseness measurement in rodents (Froudarakis et al., 2014), but our study provides the first direct measurement of sparseness of large-scale neuronal population responses, carried out in awake macaque monkeys and made possible by large-scale 2P imaging techniques.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: Earlier studies had provided life-time sparseness measurements in humans.
source: Earlier studies had provided life-time sparseness measurements in rodents (Hromádka et al., 2008; Haider et al., 2010), non-human primates (Rolls and Tovee, 1995; Vinje and Gallant, 2000; Rust and DiCarlo, 2012) and humans (Quiroga et al., 2005), as well as population sparseness measurement in rodents (Froudarakis et al., 2014), but our study provides the first direct measurement of sparseness of large-scale neuronal population responses, carried out in awake macaque monkeys and made possible by large-scale 2P imaging techniques.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: A very small ensemble of neurons from V1's superficial layer are activated at any one time in response to any given natural image.
source: We found that a very small ensemble of neurons from V1's superficial layer are activated at any one time in response to any given natural image.

claim: The small ensembles of neural responses provide a surprisingly large amount of information to downstream neurons for the discrimination of complex image patterns in natural scenes.
source: Using decoding analysis, we showed that the small ensembles of neural responses provide a surprisingly large amount of information to downstream neurons, providing for the discrimination of complex image patterns in natural scenes.

claim: Direct measurements of population sparseness are indeed comparable to life-time sparseness measurements.
source: For the first time, we have shown that direct measurements of population sparseness are indeed comparable to life-time sparseness measurements.
evidence: Comparison of two types of measurements from the study

claim: The level of sparseness observed (0.5% at half maximal response) was considerably higher than that predicted by earlier life-time estimates of sparseness based on single unit recording in macaques.
source: However, the level of sparseness that we observed (0.5% at half maximal response) was considerably higher than that predicted by the earlier life-time estimates of sparseness, which were based on single unit recording in macaques (Rust and DiCarlo, 2012).

claim: Studies on rodents have yielded a considerable range of estimates of sparseness that vary across measurement techniques.
source: Studies on rodents have yielded a considerable range of estimates of sparseness that vary across measurement techniques (Haider et al., 2010; Hromádka et al., 2008; Froudarakis et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: A single-unit study using the cell-attached patch technique showed that neurons were mostly silent in the awake auditory cortex, inferring that less than 2% of the neuronal population showed 'well-driven' responses (>20 Hz response frequency) to natural sounds.
source: A single-unit study that used the cell-attached patch technique might have been the most accurate to date (Hromádka et al., 2008), and it showed that neurons were mostly silent in the awake auditory cortex, inferring that less than 2% of the neuronal population showed 'well-driven' responses (>20 Hz response frequency) to natural sounds.
evidence: Supported by citation to Hromádka et al., 2008

claim: Neurons in the superficial layers of V1 are densely packed and have small cell bodies.
source: Our imaging shows that neurons in the superficial layers of V1 are densely packed and have small cell bodies.

claim: It may not be possible to obtain stable and well isolated single-unit signals over several hours using extracellular recording methods in superficial V1 layers.
source: Thus, it may not be possible to obtain stable and well isolated single-unit signals over several hours using extracellular recording methods.
evidence: Inference from the observation of dense packing and small cell bodies

claim: The study has reduced the biases inherent to previous extracellular recording studies in neuronal sampling, stimulus sampling, and single-cell isolation.
source: Our study has reduced the biases inherent to previous extracellular recording studies — in neuronal sampling, in stimulus sampling, and in single-cell isolation — by invoking a response in virtually all of the neurons in a single field of view and in a particular layer by using a large set of natural stimuli.
evidence: Comparison of methodology with prior approaches

claim: The high degree of population sparseness observed is consistent with the conjecture that fewer than 1% of the neurons should be substantially active concurrently in any brain area based on metabolic costs of spiking.
source: The high degree of population sparseness that we observed is consistent with two recent conjectures from theoretical neuroscience. First, based on the metabolic costs of spiking, one group posits that fewer than 1% of the neurons should be substantially active concurrently in any brain area (Lennie, 2003).

claim: Theoretical sparse-coding studies have suggested that because V1 neurons are at least 200 times more abundant than their thalamic input, V1 neurons could be quite specialized in their feature selectivity and thus highly sparse in their population responses.
source: Second, and more importantly, theoretical sparse-coding studies have suggested that because V1 neurons are at least 200 times more abundant than their thalamic input, V1 neurons could be quite specialized in their feature selectivity and thus highly sparse in their population responses (Olshausen, 2013; Rehn and Sommer, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical work

claim: V1 neurons in the superficial layers are tuned to complex patterns with a great degree of specificity.
source: We have indeed observed this very finding using 2P imaging techniques in the V1 superficial layers (Tang et al., 2018). These findings are reminiscent of the highly specific codes exhibited by neurons in the human medial temporal lobes (Quiroga et al., 2005), suggesting that many V1 neurons might be akin to highly specific 'grandmother neurons', although they may encode information in the form of an extremely sparse population code.
evidence: Supported by citation to Tang et al., 2018

claim: Many V1 neurons might be akin to highly specific 'grandmother neurons', although they may encode information in the form of an extremely sparse population code.
source: These findings are reminiscent of the highly specific codes exhibited by neurons in the human medial temporal lobes (Quiroga et al., 2005), suggesting that many V1 neurons might be akin to highly specific 'grandmother neurons', although they may encode information in the form of an extremely sparse population code.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on comparison with cited work

claim: The observed high degree of population sparseness and life-time sparseness are consistent with earlier observations that V1 neurons in this layer were tuned to complex patterns with a great degree of specificity.
source: The observed high degree of population sparseness and life-time sparseness are also consistent with our earlier observation that V1 neurons in this layer were tuned to complex patterns with a great degree of specificity (Tang et al., 2018, see also Hegdé and Van Essen, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: These findings reveal the complexity and specificity of feature selectivity and the super-sparse neural representation within a V1 hypercolumn.
source: These findings reveal the complexity and specificity of feature selectivity and the super-sparse neural representation within a V1 hypercolumn, providing new understanding of the neural codes in the macaque primary visual cortex.
evidence: Summary interpretation of the study's findings

claim: All experimental protocols were approved by the Peking University Animal Care and Use Committee.
source: All experimental protocols were approved by the Peking University Animal Care and Use Committee, and approved by the Peking University Animal Care and Use Committee (LSC-TangSM-5).

claim: The study used two adult rhesus monkeys (A and B), who were 4 and 5 years of age and weighed 5 and 7 kg, respectively.
source: The study used two adult rhesus monkeys (A and B), who were 4 and 5 years of age and weighed 5 and 7 kg, respectively (Li et al., 2017).

claim: AAV1.hSynap.GCaMP5G.WPRE.SV40 was pressure-injected at a depth of ~500 μm into the cortex.
source: The dura was opened to expose the cortex, into which 50–100 nl AAV1.hSynap.GCaMP5G.WPRE.SV40 (AV-1-PV2478, titer 2.37e13 (GC/ml), Penn Vector Core) was pressure-injected at a depth of ~500 μm.

claim: The monkeys' fixation during stimulus presentation was stable and accurate, with standard deviations smaller than 0.05°.
source: The monkeys' fixation during stimulus presentation (from 1 to 2 s in the graph) was stable and accurate. The distribution of eye positions during stimulus presentation, with standard deviations smaller than 0.05°, was significantly smaller than the typical receptive field sizes (ranging from 0.2° to 0.8°) of neurons at 3–5° eccentricities.
evidence: Measurement of eye position during experiments

claim: There were no statistically significant differences in the distribution of eye position data in weak responses, sparse strong responses, and dense responses classes.
source: We found no statistically significant differences in the distribution of eye position data in these three classes (Tang et al., 2018), indicating that the observed effects were not caused by movement differences.
evidence: Statistical analysis of eye movement data cited

claim: The observed effects were not caused by eye movement differences.
source: We found no statistically significant differences in the distribution of eye position data in these three classes (Tang et al., 2018), indicating that the observed effects were not caused by movement differences.

claim: The sparse population responses were repeatedly evoked by stimuli, and not by random eye-movement jitters.
source: The ROC and decoding analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), demonstrating the reliability of the neural responses across trials, confirm that the sparse population responses were repeatedly evoked by stimuli, and not by random eye-movement jitters.
evidence: Conclusion from ROC and decoding analysis

claim: The wavelength of the laser was set at 1000 nm for two-photon imaging.
source: The wavelength of the laser was set at 1000 nm.

claim: An area of 850 μm × 850 μm was imaged with a 16 × objective.
source: With a 16 × objective (0.8 N.A., Nikon), an area of 850 μm × 850 μm was imaged.

claim: Infected cells of up to 700 μm in depth were imaged.
source: Infected cells of up to 700 μm in depth were imaged.

claim: The study primarily focused on cells that were 160 μm to 180 μm deep, which included a high density of infected cells.
source: We primarily focused on cells that were 160 μm to 180 μm deep, which included a high density of infected cells.

claim: The cell density was high in superficial V1, and many cell bodies were quite dim at rest.
source: The cell density was high in superficial V1, and many cell bodies were quite dim at rest.

claim: It was difficult to identify cells directly by eye or by algorithm on the basis of their morphology as captured in static images.
source: It was difficult to identify these cells directly by eye or by algorithm on the basis of their morphology as captured in static images.

claim: ROIs for cell bodies were identified on the basis of their responses.
source: We therefore identified ROIs for cell bodies on the basis of their responses.

claim: More than 96% of neurons adhered to the null hypothesis (p<0.01) in the ROC analysis.
source: With this ROC analysis, we found >96% neurons that adhered to the null hypothesis (p<0.01) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).

claim: A nearest centroid classifier was used to discriminate the 2250 images on the basis of the population responses in each trial.
source: We used a nearest centroid classifier to discriminate the 2250 images on the basis of the population responses in each trial.

claim: The study provides the first direct measure of the population sparseness in awake primates.
source: Here, we employ large-scale two-photon calcium imaging to examine the responses of a large population of neurons within the superficial layers of area V1 with single-cell resolution, while simultaneously presenting a large set of natural visual stimuli, to provide the first direct measure of the population sparseness in awake primates.

claim: Only 0.5% of neurons respond strongly to any given natural image.
source: The results show that only 0.5% of neurons respond strongly to any given natural image — indicating a ten-fold increase in the inferred sparseness over previous measurements.

claim: The observed sparseness indicates a ten-fold increase in the inferred sparseness over previous measurements.
source: The results show that only 0.5% of neurons respond strongly to any given natural image — indicating a ten-fold increase in the inferred sparseness over previous measurements.

claim: These population activities are necessary and sufficient to discriminate visual stimuli with high accuracy.
source: These population activities are nevertheless necessary and sufficient to discriminate visual stimuli with high accuracy, suggesting that the neural code in the primary visual cortex is both super-sparse and highly efficient.

claim: The neural code in the primary visual cortex is both super-sparse and highly efficient.
source: These population activities are nevertheless necessary and sufficient to discriminate visual stimuli with high accuracy, suggesting that the neural code in the primary visual cortex is both super-sparse and highly efficient.
